newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman pledges action on war criminals.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman pledges action on war criminals.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman said on Thursday that any indicted war crimes suspects found in Croatia would be extradited to The Hague and he would encourage Bosnian Croats to do the same.

"Whoever has been indicted and is present in the Republic of Croatia will be delivered to the tribunal in The Hague but in Croatia there are no indicted persons held by the Croatian authorities," Tudjman told Reuters in an interview at his presidential palace in Zagreb.
"Croatia is prepared to cooperate with The Hague but it is not only Croatia who should be given such demands," he added.

Asked if he planned to use his influence to encourage Bosnian Croats to extradite indicted suspects from the staunchly pro-Croat region of Herzegovina, he said: "Certainly...But I cannot be held responsible for what is taking place in Bosnia Hercegovina."
"So far we have also brought our influence to bear on the situation over there and...I believe the results were more than good," he added.

Tudjman, who was re-elected on June 15 for a second five-year term of office and will be inaugurated later this month, looked relaxed and healthy with a fuller head of his trademark silver hair than was seen earlier this year.
U.S. officials said he was treated for a form of stomach cancer late last year but his medical council said on Saturday he had successfully completed treatment and was fit to perform all his duties.
The United States and its allies have harshly criticised Croatia for not doing enough to ensure indicted suspects are sent to the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
The tribunal has indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs (one of whom has died), 18 Croats and three Moslems -- but has only nine in its custody.

The World Bank indefinitely postponed a $30 million loan to Croatia on Tuesday after strong lobbying from the United States, which said the former Yugoslav republic had not met its peace treaty commitments sufficiently.
Tudjman dismissed U.S. allegations that Croatia was not doing enough to fulfil commitments made when he signed the Dayton peace treaty in December 1995 to end the Bosnian war.
"Concerning the Dayton accords and cooperation with the Hague tribunal, (Croatia) has been more constructive and more cooperative than the other sides involved," he said.
"Croatia will certainly remain a factor instrumental to the establishment of peace and the solution of all outstanding issues in the region."
Under Western pressure in April, Croatia extradited a war crimes suspect, Bosnian Croat Zlatko Aleksovski, for the first time.
Tudjman said he wanted to find a solution to disputes over the divided town of Mostar in western Bosnia, where Croats and Moslems have failed to establish a joint police force.
The United States cut off aid to Mostar this week because it felt Croatia was not cooperating with agreements, U.S. envoy Robert Gelbard told reporters.

"The Croats in Bosnia Hercegovina and specifically in... Mostar itself are ready to meet their commitments...Of course they would also like the other sides to be compliant with the requirements," Tudjman said.

"The problem of Mostar should not be regarded in isolation from other issues. We should pay attention and strive to implement all the provisions of the Washington and Dayton accords," he said, referring to cantonal authorities in Bosnia which have still not been fully established.
